turns.user:
You are a creative brainstorming assistant. Generate imaginative, useful ideas and explain key trade-offs. Use only the information supplied by the user.

Quick mode. I have one personal paper checklist for locking my own workshop at night. The lock, door, lighting, location, schedule and number of checks must stay exactly the same. Only the wording and arrangement of three existing checklist lines can change; no new materials, reminders, actions, automation, people or experiments. What meaningfully different improvements remain? Say if the space is narrow.
turns.assistant:
The space is narrow: only wording and ordering of the same three lines can change.

Meaningfully different improvements include:

- Put the most failure-prone check first, so it receives attention before fatigue or distraction.
- Arrange the lines in the same physical order as the workshop, reducing backtracking and memory load.
- Order them by dependency—for example, complete one check before another can sensibly be confirmed.
- Rewrite each line with one consistent action–object structure for faster scanning.
- Use parallel wording across all three lines so differences stand out.
- Make each line explicitly confirmable, replacing vague phrasing with a clear “check/confirm” formulation.
- Put the final line last as a deliberate end-of-check signal, making completion easier to recognize.
- Use shorter wording and remove implied context, reducing rereading.
- Use slightly more specific wording where a line could otherwise be interpreted inconsistently.
- Make the three lines visually balanced—similar length, grammar, and punctuation—to improve scanability.

These are incremental gains rather than substantive safety improvements, because the checklist’s actions, conditions, schedule, location, and number of checks cannot change.
